feedback: If a learner stops at the stomach as the destination, continue the journey past it and ask where nutrients actually cross into the blood and where water is removed.

If a learner describes a straight in-and-out pipe with nothing crossing into the body, focus on the small-intestine wall as a crossing point: nutrients pass through it into the blood; only the leftovers continue as waste.
If a learner says gravity moves the food down, point out you can swallow while upside down because muscles squeeze the food along.
Reinforce by asking: 'If nutrients never crossed into the blood, could the apple ever help your leg move? Why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: Digestion is not food 'vanishing in the stomach' — it is an ordered sequence that extracts nutrients into the blood at a specific place (the small intestine), while the large intestine deals with water and waste.
learnerActions: Trace the path of one mouthful out loud and in order — mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine — naming the ONE main job at each stop.
Map the journey onto your own torso with your hands as you narrate, so the sequence becomes a remembered story rather than a labelled diagram.

At the small intestine, describe the moment of insight: the useful nutrients pass THROUGH the gut wall INTO the blood, which carries them around the body (for example to the leg muscles); only the leftovers travel on.
At the large intestine, describe water being drawn back out and the remainder forming waste.
Replay the journey yourself, narrating the order and each job without prompts, to check it holds together.
activities.title: Follow your food: tracing one mouthful through the tube

feedback: If a learner thinks the intestines are short, lay the full length out so the scale is unmistakable before coiling it back up.
Connect back to the journey: most of this length is the small intestine, the long coiled part where nutrients have time to cross into the blood; the shorter, wider large intestine then removes water.
activities.intendedInsight: The intestines are several metres long and coiled up inside the belly, not short — this corrects the idea that digestion happens in one small bag.
learnerActions: Unroll roughly a 7-metre length of string or rope to represent the intestines, then coil it into a small space to show how they pack into the belly.
Compare this length against your own height and against the small 'tummy' many children imagine.
Explain in your own words why 'the tummy is one small bag' is wrong — the gut is a very long, coiled tube.
activities.title: How long are the intestines really?

feedback: If a learner says food 'dissolves into nothing', point to the mash left in the bag: it is broken down, and the useful part is later absorbed while the rest becomes waste.
If a learner credits gravity for moving food, relate the tights-squeeze model to swallowing upside down.
activities.intendedInsight: Digestion involves physical breakdown and movement driven by teeth and muscle action, plus chemical help from saliva, stomach acid and digestive juices — food is actively worked on, not simply dissolved into nothing.
learnerActions: Mash a cracker with a little water inside a sealed bag to model how the stomach churns food with acid into a mush.
Push a small soft object along inside a length of tights/stocking to model how muscles squeeze food along the tube (peristalsis).

Say that both models show physical breaking-down and moving (churning, squeezing), then name the chemical help in the real body that the models do not show (saliva, stomach acid and other digestive juices), so digestion is understood as both, not as magic.
activities.title: Hands-on models of the mechanical steps

feedback: Full understanding: nutrients are absorbed through the small-intestine wall into the blood, which carries them to the muscles, and the large intestine is distinguished as removing water and forming waste.
Partial: lists the organs in order and says food is 'broken down' but can't explain absorption — prompt specifically for where nutrients pass into the blood.
Gap: describes a straight-through pipe (mouth to toilet) with nothing crossing into the body, or names only the stomach — return to the small-intestine wall as the crossing point.
Probe further: 'Is the large intestine absorbing nutrients too, or doing a different job?' and 'If nutrients never crossed into the blood, could the apple help your leg move?'
activities.intendedInsight: Only a learner who grasps absorption into the blood can bridge gut to muscle; stating where nutrients cross and distinguishing the large intestine's water-and-waste job shows real understanding.
learnerActions: Answer: 'After you eat an apple, some of it ends up helping your leg muscles work, and some comes out later as waste. How does a bit of the apple get all the way from inside your tummy to your leg? Talk me through the journey and explain how the useful part gets there.'
Point to WHERE the useful part leaves the gut and enters the blood.
Say whether the large intestine absorbs nutrients too, or does a different job, and name that job.
activities.title: Explain-the-journey diagnostic: apple to leg muscle

feedback: If a learner describes food and liquid taking different internal routes, clarify the single shared tract: water is absorbed through the intestine walls along the way, with the large intestine drawing the remaining water out of the leftovers.
If a learner names the stomach as where waste is made, trace onward to the large intestine where the leftovers form waste.
activities.intendedInsight: Digestion happens in one continuous tract; waste is formed in the large intestine, not the stomach, and there is no second internal food/drink pipe.
learnerActions: Explain that the digestive tract is ONE continuous food tube from mouth to the end — not a separate pipe for food and another for drink.

Say that water travels along the same tube as food and is absorbed through the intestine walls (much of it in the small intestine, with the large intestine drawing back the remaining water from the leftovers), rather than imagining it carried by a second internal pipe.
Correct the idea that 'the stomach is where poo is made' by naming the large intestine as where waste is formed, after nutrients and water have been removed.
activities.title: One shared food tube, not two pipes
